targets: Septal branches of anterior interventricular artery
title: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and alcohol septal ablation
text:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (autosomal dominant sarcomere mutations, most often MYH7 or MYBPC3) causes asymmetric septal hypertrophy. In the obstructive form the thick basal septum and systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral leaflet obstruct the left ventricular outflow tract: an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that gets LOUDER with Valsalva or standing (less preload) and quieter with squatting or handgrip. It is the classic cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.
The septal perforating branches of the anterior interventricular artery supply the anterior two-thirds of the septum, including the bundle of His and right bundle branch. Alcohol septal ablation injects ethanol into the first septal perforator to infarct the obstructing septum; the main complication is complete heart block needing a pacemaker. The same anatomy explains why a proximal LAD occlusion can cause new right or left bundle branch block.

targets: Right inferolateral branch of right coronary artery
title: Right ventricular infarction
text:
The right ventricular (acute marginal) branches leave the proximal right coronary artery, so an occlusion before them infarcts the right ventricle as well as the inferior wall, in about a third of inferior infarcts. The thin right ventricle fails as a passive conduit: hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and Kussmaul sign with CLEAR lung fields.
ST elevation in right-sided lead V4R confirms it, so right-sided leads should be recorded in every inferior STEMI. Output is preload dependent: nitrates, morphine and diuretics can cause profound hypotension; treatment is IV fluid and urgent reperfusion. Isolated RV infarction is rare because the RV has low oxygen demand and collateral supply from the LAD via the moderator band artery.

title: Aortic cusps, coronary ostia and aortic root abscess
text:
The coronary arteries arise from the right and left aortic sinuses of Valsalva, just above the right and left coronary cusps; the non-coronary (posterior) cusp has no ostium. Coronary filling occurs mainly in diastole, which is one reason aortic regurgitation and tachycardia worsen ischaemia.
The non-coronary cusp and the adjacent right cusp sit on the membranous septum next to the atrioventricular node and bundle of His. Aortic valve endocarditis that burrows into the root (root abscess) therefore shows up as a new prolonged PR interval or heart block on ECG, a strong indication for surgery. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation can likewise cause heart block, and a bulky cusp pushed aside can occlude a low coronary ostium.
A bicuspid valve (1 to 2% of people, usually right-left cusp fusion) is linked to coarctation, Turner syndrome and dilatation of the ascending aorta. A ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm (usually the right sinus into the right ventricle or atrium) produces a sudden continuous murmur and heart failure.

title: Marfan syndrome and aortic root dilatation
text:
Fibrillin-1 mutations weaken the aortic media (cystic medial degeneration), causing annuloaortic ectasia: a pear-shaped dilatation that begins at the sinuses of Valsalva and effaces the sinotubular junction. The results are aortic regurgitation and type A dissection. Patients have serial echocardiography or MRI, take beta-blockers or angiotensin receptor blockers, and have prophylactic root replacement (often valve-sparing) at about 5.0 cm, earlier with a family history of dissection, rapid growth or planned pregnancy.
Other Marfan features: tall stature with arm span exceeding height, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity, upward (superotemporal) lens dislocation, mitral valve prolapse and spontaneous pneumothorax. Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGF-beta receptor mutations, bifid uvula, arterial tortuosity) dissects at smaller diameters. Tertiary syphilis also dilates the ascending aorta (tree-bark intima, obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum).

title: Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale
text:
Pulmonary hypertension is a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg at rest on right heart catheterisation. Causes are grouped as pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic, BMPR2, connective tissue disease, drugs, congenital shunts), left heart disease (commonest), lung disease and hypoxia, chronic thromboembolic disease and miscellaneous.
Signs reflect the pressure-loaded right heart: a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, left parasternal heave, raised JVP with giant v waves from tricuspid regurgitation, peripheral oedema (cor pulmonale) and sometimes the early diastolic Graham Steell murmur of pulmonary regurgitation. The chest radiograph shows enlarged central pulmonary arteries with peripheral 'pruning', and CT shows a pulmonary trunk wider than the ascending aorta. Chronic thromboembolic disease is potentially curable by pulmonary endarterectomy.

title: Patent ductus arteriosus and duct-dependent lesions
text:
The ductus arteriosus joins the pulmonary trunk at the origin of the left pulmonary artery to the underside of the aortic arch just beyond the left subclavian artery, shunting blood away from the fetal lungs. Rising oxygen tension and falling prostaglandin E2 close it functionally within one to three days; it becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, around which the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks (at risk during duct ligation).
Persistence is common in premature babies and after congenital rubella: a continuous 'machinery' murmur below the left clavicle, bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure; left-to-right shunting leads to heart failure and eventually Eisenmenger physiology with differential cyanosis of the toes. Closure uses indomethacin, ibuprofen or paracetamol, or catheter devices.
Conversely, in duct-dependent lesions (transposition, pulmonary atresia, critical coarctation, hypoplastic left heart) the duct must be kept open with a prostaglandin E1 infusion, and neonatal collapse at day two to three is the sign that it is closing.

title: Transposition of the great arteries and truncus arteriosus
text:
When the aorticopulmonary (spiral) septum fails to spiral, the aorta arises from the right ventricle anteriorly and the pulmonary trunk from the left ventricle: two parallel circulations. The neonate is profoundly cyanosed within hours and survives only through mixing across the ductus arteriosus, foramen ovale or a VSD. Chest radiograph: narrow mediastinum, 'egg on a string'. Maternal diabetes is a risk factor.
Management is prostaglandin E1 to keep the duct open, balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind) to improve mixing, then the arterial switch operation in the first weeks with reimplantation of the coronary arteries.
If the septum fails to form at all, a single truncus arteriosus overrides a VSD (associated with 22q11 deletion); tetralogy of Fallot results from anterior displacement of the same septum.

targets: Septal leaflet of right atrioventricular valve
title: Ebstein anomaly
text:
The septal and inferior (posterior) leaflets of the tricuspid valve are displaced apically, so part of the right ventricle is 'atrialised'. The result is tricuspid regurgitation, a huge right atrium (a box-shaped cardiac silhouette on chest radiograph) and a small functional right ventricle. Most patients have an atrial septal defect or patent foramen ovale, through which right-to-left shunting causes cyanosis and paradoxical embolism.
Accessory pathways (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) accompany it in up to a quarter of cases, causing re-entrant tachycardias. Maternal lithium use has been associated with it, although the risk is small. Severity ranges from fetal hydrops to discovery in adulthood.

title: Ablation landmarks: triangle of Koch and cavotricuspid isthmus
text:
The sinoatrial node lies at the junction of the superior vena cava with the right atrium, at the top of the crista terminalis. The atrioventricular node sits at the apex of the triangle of Koch, bounded by the tendon of Todaro, the attachment of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve and the ostium of the coronary sinus at its base.
In AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia the 'slow pathway' runs near the coronary sinus ostium, so it is ablated low in the triangle; ablating too high risks complete heart block from injury to the compact node.
Typical atrial flutter (sawtooth waves in II, III, aVF at an atrial rate of about 300/min, often 2:1 block giving a ventricular rate of 150) circulates counterclockwise around the tricuspid annulus. A line of ablation across the cavotricuspid isthmus, between the inferior vena cava and the tricuspid annulus, cures it in most patients.

targets: Anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle
Septal papillary muscle of right ventricle
title: Moderator band and bundle branch block
text:
The septomarginal trabecula (moderator band) crosses the right ventricular cavity from the septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle, carrying the right bundle branch so that the papillary muscle tightens its chordae before the ventricle contracts. It is a landmark identifying the morphological right ventricle on echocardiography and a site from which ventricular ectopy can arise. The small septal papillary muscle lies close to where the right bundle emerges beneath the septal leaflet.
The right bundle branch is a thin single fascicle, easily blocked by right ventricular strain, pulmonary embolism, an atrial septal defect or a pulmonary artery catheter: RSR' ('M') pattern in V1 with a broad slurred S in V6. Left bundle branch block (broad notched R in V6, deep S in V1) nearly always indicates structural heart disease and makes ST segments hard to interpret in suspected infarction (Sgarbossa criteria).

title: Mechanical complications after myocardial infarction
text:
Timing points to the lesion. First 24 hours: ventricular fibrillation and other arrhythmias, the commonest cause of early death. Days 2 to 7, when the necrotic myocardium is softest (macrophage phase): papillary muscle rupture with acute pulmonary oedema and new mitral regurgitation (posteromedial muscle after inferior infarction), ventricular septal rupture with a new pansystolic murmur and step-up in oxygen saturation in the right ventricle, and free wall rupture with haemopericardium and tamponade, typically in elderly women after a first transmural infarct.
Weeks later: a true left ventricular aneurysm (thin fibrous scar, persistent ST elevation, mural thrombus and embolic stroke, ventricular tachycardia), or a pseudoaneurysm, a contained rupture with a narrow neck that needs surgery. Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis two to ten weeks after infarction.

title: Cardiomegaly and heart failure on the chest radiograph
text:
On a posteroanterior radiograph a cardiothoracic ratio above 0.5 suggests cardiomegaly; an anteroposterior (portable, supine) film magnifies the heart and cannot be used this way. Causes include dilated cardiomyopathy (idiopathic, alcohol, anthracyclines such as doxorubicin, viral myocarditis from Coxsackie B, peripartum, genetic titin mutations), valve disease, ischaemic heart disease and a pericardial effusion, which gives a globular 'water-bottle' silhouette with clear lungs.
The radiographic signs of left heart failure are remembered as ABCDE: Alveolar oedema in a perihilar 'bat's wing' distribution, Kerley B lines (thickened interlobular septa at the costophrenic angles), Cardiomegaly, Dilated upper lobe vessels (upper lobe diversion) and pleural Effusions, often bilateral and larger on the right.

title: Kawasaki disease and anomalous coronary arteries
text:
Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of children under five: fever for five days or more with bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, red cracked lips and strawberry tongue, cervical lymphadenopathy, polymorphous rash and red swollen hands and feet that later peel. Untreated, about a quarter develop coronary artery aneurysms; intravenous immunoglobulin within ten days (with aspirin, a rare paediatric indication) cuts this to about 5%. Giant aneurysms of 8 mm or more can thrombose, causing myocardial infarction in childhood or early adult life, so echocardiography is essential.
Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA, Bland-White-Garland syndrome) causes infant infarction with irritability and sweating during feeds as pulmonary pressure falls. A coronary artery arising from the wrong sinus and running between the aorta and pulmonary trunk can be compressed during exercise and is a recognised cause of sudden death in young athletes.

title: Takayasu arteritis
text:
A granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of young women (under 40, commoner in Asia) that narrows the aortic arch and its branches: 'pulseless disease'. Presentation is a systemic illness (fever, weight loss, raised ESR) followed by arm claudication, absent or unequal radial pulses, a blood pressure difference between the arms, subclavian and carotid bruits, visual disturbance and syncope. Involvement of the renal arteries causes hypertension, and aortic root dilatation causes aortic regurgitation.
Diagnosis is by MR or CT angiography (long smooth stenoses, wall thickening) or PET; treatment is corticosteroids with steroid-sparing agents, and angioplasty or bypass for fixed stenoses. Giant cell arteritis affects the same vessels but in patients over 50.

title: Anomalous pulmonary venous return
text:
Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return most often drains the right superior pulmonary vein into the superior vena cava, and nearly always accompanies a sinus venosus atrial septal defect near the SVC orifice. It produces a left-to-right shunt with right heart dilatation. In scimitar syndrome the right pulmonary veins descend to the inferior vena cava, forming a curved 'Turkish sword' shadow beside the right heart border, with a hypoplastic right lung and dextroposition of the heart.
In total anomalous pulmonary venous return all the pulmonary veins drain to the systemic venous side (supracardiac to the innominate vein, giving a 'snowman' silhouette; cardiac to the coronary sinus; or infracardiac through the diaphragm to the portal system). Survival depends on an atrial septal communication, and the obstructed infracardiac type is a neonatal surgical emergency with severe cyanosis and pulmonary oedema.

title: Auscultation areas versus the valves themselves
text:
The valves lie close together behind the sternum along an oblique line from the third left costal cartilage to the sixth right costal cartilage: the pulmonary valve highest (behind the third left costal cartilage), then the aortic, mitral (behind the fourth left costal cartilage) and tricuspid (behind the sternum at the fourth intercostal space). Sounds are best heard where blood carries them downstream: aortic area at the second right intercostal space, pulmonary area at the second left, tricuspid area at the lower left sternal edge and mitral area at the apex (fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line).
Manoeuvres: inspiration augments right-sided murmurs (Carvallo sign); the left lateral decubitus position brings out mitral stenosis with the bell; sitting forward in held expiration brings out aortic regurgitation at the left sternal edge. Aortic stenosis radiates to the carotids and mitral regurgitation to the axilla. A displaced apex beat implies left ventricular dilatation.
